Truck Wars

By: Jacqui Jayamaha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
About 88% of goods in SA are transported by road with 50% transported via the N3. The escalating incidents of attacks on freight trucks is having a massive impact on the economy.

Unique Selling Point:
The trucking industry is under attack and bleeding. The freight industry in SA is the blood of the country as staples such as bread, milk and fuel comes to us via the trucking sector. The trucking industry is a bigger contributor to the country than Eskom - if the current status quo continues prices will escalate rapidly impacting further on an already stretched economy and on those living in poverty. The huge psychological impact these attacks are having on drivers and their families. The chaos at the Port of Durban and the perception from international import / export groups that South Africa is a major risk destination/business partner.

Summary:
We look at why this massive escalation of attacks on the trucking industry is occurring and the huge knock on effects this will have in the country. Drivers are being shot at and their freights, petrol bombed in attacks that are seeming more like targeted ambush attempts. Who is behind these attacks and where did it all begin and why? We interview major players in our SA Trucking industry and logistics planners, to find out what exactly is at the root of these deadly onslaughts and what solutions are on offer to calm this already raging storm. Minister Bheki Cele has called this "Economic Sabotage" we ask him to clarify these comments and share solutions. What has been implemented after the meeting, what steps have been taken going forward? Is there organised crime involved and are trucks being sabotaged to benefit a group of major players in the logistics industry.

Further information:
The reality is - Everything we see in our retail stores has had to 'get there' - without the trucking and freight industry our goods would not be delivered for us the consumers. Has the government invested in the necessary skills development of local drivers in order to put them behind the wheel transporting hazardous materials? Why have foreign national drivers been targeted when they have all the necessary training and skills and SA home affairs permits? What is at the root of this unrest?

Press Release:


Truck Wars
“Avoid being on the N3 at night” – that’s the alarming warning from authorities as violent attacks on freight trucks continue to escalate country-wide and especially on the N3 trade route linking Durban and Johannesburg. But with 88% of goods in South Africa being transported by road, and almost 50% on this route alone, this national stretch of highway is the lifeblood of the logistics system and the backbone of the economy. As government scrambles to deal with the armed assailants targeting truck drivers, Carte Blanche investigates the real reasons behind the violence that’s crippling the industry.
Producer: Jacqui Jayamaha
Presenter: Devi Sankaree Govender


Script:


Truck Wars Final Script
Script Visual
VO: It’s early morning in June, on the N3 just outside of Pietermaritzburg.
Two freight trucks carrying hazardous materials from a depot near Durban harbour, heading to Johannesburg, lie in ruins.
Overnight the trucks were shot at and petrol-bombed by unknown assailants.
The heat from fire was so intense that it melted the tyres into the tar road. Both drivers were lucky to escape with their lives… Aerials and signs
Smaller typed graphics
UPSOUND Local Driver : There was a white double cab vehicle that passed us shooting, so as soon as he passed us he stopped in the front and started shooting again, this is what a seat used to be like and I just jumped out activated the hand brake and off I went, I had to do what I did or else I would have been dead…
Aerial shots of Durban harbour…
LINK: Durban is one of the busiest ports in South Africa. It is the second largest container port in Africa in Southern Hemisphere.
V/O About 88% of goods in South Africa are transported by road and the N3 corridor is the major truck freight route from Durban to Johannesburg. Almost 50% of goods are transported along this route.
It’s the main artery and lifeblood of the logistics system... but it’s also on this stretch of the highway, where hundreds of freight trucks come under attack.
Survivors, many of them fearing for their lives, refuse to show their faces on camera.
Driver 2 I feared for my life, I heard more gun shots, I thought the other driver was dead already, how do you work like this, fearing for our lives.
V/O In the last year there have been numerous attacks on trucks and their drivers. The Road Freight Association, voice of the trucking industry in South Africa, estimates that close to 1 400 trucks across the country have either been burnt, damaged or destroyed. More than 20 drivers have been killed.
Link: Imagine what it feels like for drivers as they get into large freighters and set out on a journey to deliver their cargo all across the country? They leave not knowing if they will return home, literally putting their lives on the line to earn a living.
VO: Since April alone, 60 trucks have been torched countrywide, seventeen of those just this month in KwaZulu-Natal.
UPSOUND Bheki Cele It’s a huge crime … for us as the South African police, it’s economic sabotage.
VO: Police Minister Bheki Cele says it’s difficult to pinpoint who’s responsible for the violence…
UPSOUND Bheki Cele: 03.23 Sometimes it’s the communities initiating those things … Sometimes it’s a collaboration between drivers and the communities that will come and ….around these highways.
VO: To date 91 suspects have been arrested. The motives remain unclear but the economic impact will be felt long after the authorities get this under control.
UPSOUND Mike Schussler This is economic terrorism against the people of South Africa
V/O Transport and freight specialist economist, Mike Schussler warns that the fiscal impact of the truck wars on the country is severe.
UPSOUND Mike Schussler: If we look at road freight for transporting other peoples goods that was R121 billion last year, so that’s a large part of the SA economy, but that’s not all coz many people are transporting for themselves so you could close to double this.
VO: It seems the problem has roots. Advocate Pria Hassan of the Positive Freight Solutions Forum, that represents about 3000 vehicles and 250 owners, says the violence started as protests against trucking companies, accused of hiring too many foreign nationals.
A petrol bomb attack left this Zimbabwean driver with severe burns.
But South African drivers have also become collateral damage in the war, like Bernard Groenewald, a trucker from the Western Cape, who recently succumbed to his burn injuries.
UPSOUND Advocate Pria Hassan: The reality that in 1996 and even prior to that we opened our doors to foreigners to allow them to work in South Africa, the job creation issue now with the amount of foreigners in the country has become somewhat of a huge conflict. Positive freight solutions is committed to try and find a way in which we swing the unemployment ratios back to our people.
VO: Hassan says evidence suggests that the “All Truck Drivers Foundation” or ATDF, with mostly unemployed South African drivers as members, are responsible for attacks.
UPSOUND Devi: How do we know for sure that some of the attacks are coming from an ATDF point of view?
UPSOUND Adv. Hassan: This has been thoroughly investigated, we’ve had members from the ATDF approach our depots storm our depots stop our trucks, intimidate our drivers. There is a warning prior to something happening it comes via the ATDF chats. They visit our sites, we can’t do what they want us to do, then our members have their trucks burnt – with in the space of 7 days.
VO: But the Chairperson of the ATDF, Sipho Zungu, insists that his members have done nothing wrong.
UPSOUND Devi So their argument is that members of your organisation are orchestrating trouble and violence.
UPSOUND Zungu Ok our members have been going to a number of companies, asking the employers tell them what we’re fighting for asking the employers to employ citizens, they go in the companies they raise these our voices and they go.
UPSOUND Devi So you’re saying that’s not meant to be intimidating? Have done
UPSOUND Devi Do you phone the people up and say we’d like to come and have a chat or do you just pitch up?
UPSOUND Zungu My guys just pitch up they don’t phone to tell people we are coming, because the reason being there is foreign nationals - they will chase the foreign nationals or they will hide them and say “Check here, there’s no foreign nationals”.
VO: We played Zungu a voice message intercepted from one of ATDF’s own chat groups…
Play recording Translation “The war has started against the ADFT, they are busy protecting their rubbish of hiring foreigners, they must f*cking go and die out of the country, out of South Africa.”
UPSOUND Devi Whose voice is that?
UPSOUND Zungu: Sifiso Nyathi
VO: Sifiso Nyathi is the Secretary General of ATDF and Zungu’s right hand man.
UPSOUND Devi This kind of talk is the kind of talk that causes even bigger problems.
UPSOUND Zungu the people I am leading are hungry and angry.
UPSOUND Devi Do you think that anger could make people just go out and burn trucks?
UPSOUND Zungu So people when they are angry, they can do anything.
VO: As tensions between drivers continue to intensify, Gavin Kelly CEO of the Road Freight Association that represents freight drivers believes mediation should help ease the situation. RFA logo
UPSOUND Devi If you have SA drivers who are saying, “Hang one we are not being employed because the foreigners who are employed are here already illegally?
UPSOUND Gavin There’s surely an easier way to fix that we don’t need to burn trucks to do that. We could have some sort of a discussion between the parties.
UPSOUND Adv. Hassan We’ve issued an interdict against ATDF because it was the ATDF that visited out sites.
VO: Hoping to relieve the chaos in the industry, Positive Freight Solutions has asked the court to grant a final interdict preventing the ATDF form entering their premises and intimidating or assaulting their drivers. The court will rule on the 18th of July.
From government’s side, Cele has deployed more teams to control the violence.
UPSOUND Bheki Cele: 09.47 We have increased and made police visibility for 550 kilometers that would be from JHB to DBN … There are sometimes cameras along the roads, and we are collecting that evidence
VO: Meanwhile, police have identified two suspects in the early June attack outside Pietermaritzburg.
Both suspects are members of the ATDF—and one has since shot himself.
But as the violence continues, its ordinary South Africans who bear the economic brunt.
UPSOUND Mike Schussler: 07.24 If you look at the knock on effect into the country its in the billions and …if we carry on with this it’s going to be in the hundreds of billions”

PROMO 1
Violent armed attacks on truck drivers persist country-wide as road freight companies struggle to find ways to ensure employees’ safety at work. Can authorities defuse rising tensions?

PROMO 2
We investigate the escalation of violent, armed attacks on truck drivers country-wide as road freight companies struggle to find ways of assuring employees’ safety.

PROMO 3
Despite government plans to deal with armed attacks on trucks, the frequency of violent and random firing on truckers persists. We investigate what motivates these attacks.

Minister Bheki Cele has called this "Economic Sabotage" we ask him to clarify these comments and share solutions. What has been implemented after the meeting, what steps have been taken going forward? Is there organised crime involved and are trucks being sabotaged to benefit a group of major players in the logistics industry.
metadata.Further information: The reality is - Everything we see in our retail stores has had to 'get there' - without the trucking and freight industry our goods would not be delivered for us the consumers. Has the government invested in the necessary skills development of local drivers in order to put them behind the wheel transporting hazardous materials? Why have foreign national drivers been targeted when they have all the necessary training and skills and SA home affairs permits? What is at the root of this unrest?
